name: C++ Core Concepts
description: Memory model, object lifetime, move semantics and the rules that bite in production code.

cards.front: What is RAII, and what problem does it solve?
cards.back: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: a resource's lifetime is tied to the lifetime of an object. The constructor acquires, the destructor releases. Because destructors run deterministically during stack unwinding, resources are freed correctly even when an exception is thrown.

cards.front: What is the difference between `std::move` and an actual move?
cards.back: `std::move` performs no move at all — it is only a cast to an rvalue reference. It makes the argument *eligible* for a move; whether anything moves depends on the overload selected and on the type having a move constructor or move assignment operator.

cards.front: What is the state of an object after it has been moved from?
cards.back: Valid but unspecified. You may destroy it or assign a new value to it, but you must not rely on its contents. Standard library types additionally guarantee they are left in a state where all operations with no preconditions are still safe.

cards.front: What is the Rule of Five?
cards.back: If you declare any one of the destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, or move assignment, you should consider declaring all five, because declaring one suppresses the implicit generation of others. The Rule of Zero is better: design so you need none of them.

cards.front: Why must a base class destructor be `virtual` when deleting through a base pointer?
cards.back: Without a virtual destructor, `delete basePtr` on an object of derived type is undefined behavior. The dynamic type's destructor is never invoked, so derived members leak and derived invariants are never torn down.

cards.front: What is the difference between `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr` in cost terms?
cards.back: `unique_ptr` is zero-overhead: it is the size of a raw pointer with no atomic operations. `shared_ptr` carries a second pointer to a control block and performs atomic increments and decrements on the reference count, which costs both memory and cache traffic under contention.

cards.front: What is a data race, and how does it differ from a race condition?
cards.back: A data race is two threads accessing the same memory location concurrently where at least one access is a write and none are synchronized — this is undefined behavior in C++. A race condition is the broader logical bug where program correctness depends on timing; it can exist even in fully synchronized code.

It lets the compiler omit exception-handling scaffolding, and it lets library code select more efficient paths. Notably `std::vector` reallocation will move elements instead of copying only when the move constructor is `noexcept`. If a `noexcept` function does throw, `std::terminate` is called.

cards.front: Why is `std::vector` usually faster than `std::list` for traversal, even for insertions in the middle?
cards.back: Contiguous storage gives spatial locality, so the hardware prefetcher works and each cache line carries many elements. A linked list chases pointers, incurring a likely cache miss per node. The memmove cost of a vector insertion is often cheaper than the accumulated misses.

cards.front: What is the difference between `const` applied to a pointer versus the pointee?
cards.back: `const T* p` — the pointee is const, the pointer can be reseated. `T* const p` — the pointer is const, the pointee is mutable. Read declarations right to left. `const T* const p` makes both const.

cards.front: What is the static initialization order problem?
cards.back: The initialization order of non-local static objects across different translation units is unspecified, so one may be used before it is constructed. The usual fix is the function-local static (Meyers singleton), which is initialized on first use and is thread-safe since C++11.

It stops the constructor from being used for implicit conversions and copy-initialization, so `Foo f = 42;` fails while `Foo f(42);` still works. This prevents surprising conversions in overload resolution.

cards.front: What is return value optimization, and what changed in C++17?
cards.back: RVO elides the copy or move when returning a temporary. In C++17 this became mandatory for the pure case: returning a prvalue constructs directly into the caller's storage, so no copy or move constructor need even exist. Named RVO remains a permitted-but-optional optimization.

cards.front: Why is it undefined behavior to read from a union member other than the one last written?
cards.back: Only one member is alive at a time; writing one member ends the lifetime of the others. Reading an inactive member is type punning, which the standard does not permit. Use `std::memcpy` or, since C++20, `std::bit_cast` for reinterpreting bits.

cards.front: What is the difference between `std::atomic` with `memory_order_relaxed` and `memory_order_seq_cst`?
cards.back: `relaxed` guarantees only atomicity of the operation itself, with no ordering constraints on surrounding operations, so it is cheap. `seq_cst` establishes a single total order observed by all threads, typically requiring a full memory barrier and making it the most expensive ordering.
